USMLE-style practice · Clinical medicine

Regular narrow complexes without sinus P waves

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

An asymptomatic adult’s ECG shows a regular rhythm at 48/min with narrow QRS complexes. Small inverted P waves appear immediately after each QRS in the inferior leads. Which rhythm best explains this pattern?

  1. Junctional escape rhythm
  2. Atrial fibrillation
  3. Sinus tachycardia
  4. Ventricular escape rhythm
  5. Atrial flutter with variable conduction
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Junctional escape rhythm

The slow regular narrow-complex rhythm with retrograde atrial activation is consistent with a junctional escape focus.

Understanding the options

Junctional escape rhythm
The slow regular narrow-complex rhythm with retrograde atrial activation is consistent with a junctional escape focus.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation typically produces an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia is faster and has normal sinus P waves preceding QRS complexes.
Ventricular escape rhythm
A ventricular escape is generally slower with broad QRS complexes, absent special conduction circumstances.
Atrial flutter with variable conduction
Flutter usually shows organized rapid atrial activity rather than one retrograde P wave per beat.
